questions.question: Which of the following is/are Bottom-Up Parser(s)?
questions.explanation:
Bottom-up parsers build the parse tree from the leaves up to the root using reductions: shift-reduce parsers, operator precedence parser and the LR family (LR(0), SLR, LALR, CLR).

Predictive parser and LL(1) parser are top-down parsers.

Answer: Shift-reduce Parser, LR Parser

questions.question: Which one of the following statements is FALSE?

options.A: Context-free grammar can be used to specify both lexical and syntax rules.
options.B: Type checking is done before parsing.
options.C: High-level language programs can be translated to different Intermediate Representations.
options.D: Arguments to a function can be passed using the program stack.

questions.explanation:
Type checking is part of semantic analysis, which comes after parsing (it needs the syntax tree). So "type checking is done before parsing" is false. The other statements are true.

Answer: Type checking is done before parsing

questions.question:
Consider the following statements.

S1: The sequence of procedure calls corresponds to a preorder traversal of the activation tree.
S2: The sequence of procedure returns corresponds to a postorder traversal of the activation tree.

Which one of the following options is correct?

options.A: S1 is true and S2 is false
options.B: S1 is false and S2 is true
options.C: S1 is true and S2 is true
options.D: S1 is false and S2 is false

questions.explanation:
In an activation tree a procedure is called (visited) before its children [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] calls follow preorder. A procedure returns only after all its children return [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] returns follow postorder.

questions.question:
Which of the following statements are CORRECT?
1) Static allocation of all data areas by a compiler makes it impossible to implement recursion.
2) Automatic garbage collection is essential to implement recursion.
3) Dynamic allocation of activation records is essential to implement recursion.
4) Both heap and stack are essential to implement recursion.
questions.explanation:
Checking each statement:
- 1: With static allocation each function has one fixed data area, so recursive calls overwrite it [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] True.
- 2: Garbage collection is not needed for recursion [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] False.
- 3: Each call needs its own activation record created at run time [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] True.
- 4: A stack alone is enough; a heap is not needed [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] False.

Answer: 1 and 3 only

questions.question:
Consider the following two syntax-directed definitions [latex]\text{SDD1}[/latex] and [latex]\text{SDD2}[/latex] for type declarations.

[latex] \begin{array}{|l|l|} \hline {\textbf{SDD1}} \\ \hline { \begin{array}{c} \textbf{Grammar} \\ (G_1) \end{array}} & {\textbf{Semantic Rules}} \\ \hline \hline D \rightarrow TV & \begin{array}{l} D.type = T.type \\ V.type = T.type \end{array} \\ \hline T \rightarrow \text{int} & T.type = \text{int} \\ \hline T \rightarrow \text{float} & T.type = \text{float} \\ \hline V \rightarrow V_1\ \text{id} & \begin{array}{l} V_1.type = V.type \\ \text{put(id.entry, V.type)} \end{array} \\ \hline V \rightarrow \text{id} & \text{put(id.entry, V.type)} \\ \hline \end{array} [/latex]

[latex] \begin{array}{|l|l|} \hline {\textbf{SDD2}} \\ \hline { \begin{array}{c} \textbf{Grammar} \\ (G_2) \end{array}} & {\textbf{Semantic Rules}} \\ \hline \hline D \rightarrow D_1\ \text{id} & \begin{array}{l} D.type = D_1.type \\ \text{put(id.entry, }D_1.type) \end{array} \\ \hline D \rightarrow T\ \text{id} & \begin{array}{l} D.type = T.type \\ \text{put(id.entry, T.type)} \end{array} \\ \hline T \rightarrow \text{int} & T.type = \text{int} \\ \hline T \rightarrow \text{float} & T.type = \text{float} \\ \hline \end{array} [/latex]

[latex]D[/latex] is the start symbol, and int, float and id are the three terminals. The non-terminal [latex]V_{1}[/latex] is the same as [latex]V[/latex] and the non-terminal [latex]D_{1}[/latex] is the same as [latex]D[/latex]. Here, the subscript is used to differentiate the grammar symbols on the two sides of a production. The function put updates the symbol table with the type information for an identifier.

Let [latex]\text{P}[/latex] and [latex]\text{Q}[/latex] be the languages specified by grammars [latex]\text{G1}[/latex] and [latex]\text{G2}[/latex], respectively. Which of the following statements is/are true?

options.A: The languages P and Q are the same
options.B: SSD2 is S-attributed and contains only synthesized attributes
options.C: SSD1 is L-attributed and contains only inherited attributes
options.D: The specifications of SSD1 and SSD2 are such that the same entries get added to the symbol table

questions.explanation:
Language equivalence: [latex]G_1[/latex] generates a type keyword followed by one-or-more identifiers (via the recursive [latex]V[/latex]); [latex]G_2[/latex] generates the same thing via a left-recursive [latex]D[/latex]. Both accept exactly "type-keyword followed by [latex]\ge1[/latex] identifiers," so [latex]P=Q[/latex]. True.

SDD2's attribute style: In SDD2, [latex]D.type[/latex] and the [latex]\text{put}[/latex] actions are all computed purely from the values of the symbols on the right-hand side of each production (children of the node in the parse tree) — every attribute is synthesized, making SDD2 S-attributed. True.

SDD1's attribute style: In SDD1, [latex]V.type[/latex] is set from [latex]T.type[/latex] (an inherited value flowing top-down from the parent [latex]D[/latex] into [latex]V[/latex], then further down into [latex]V_1[/latex]), so SDD1 does use inherited attributes — but [latex]D.type[/latex] itself is synthesized from [latex]T.type[/latex] as well, so SDD1 is L-attributed but it is not true that it contains "only" inherited attributes (it has both kinds). False as stated.

Symbol table contents: In SDD1, [latex]\text{put(id.entry, V.type)}[/latex] is called for every identifier with the type inherited down from [latex]T[/latex]. In SDD2, [latex]\text{put(id.entry, ...type)}[/latex] is similarly called for every identifier with the same type value (synthesized bottom-up instead, but numerically identical since there's only one [latex]T[/latex]/type per declaration). Since both add exactly one entry per identifier with the same type value, the symbol tables end up identical. True.

Answer: P and Q are the same language; SDD2 is S-attributed with only synthesized attributes; and both SDDs populate the symbol table with the same entries.
